name: The Rise of the Papacy

objectives.text: Identify the pope as the bishop who led the church in the city of Rome
Locate Rome on a map and name it as the capital city of the Roman Empire
Retell what Scripture records about Paul preaching in Rome and Jesus foretelling Peter's death, and recall the early church's report that both apostles died there
Identify from Scripture that Jesus Christ is the head of the church
Describe how the bishop of Rome came to be called pope, a title meaning father
Explain how Leo the Great's meeting with Attila the Hun in 452 raised the standing of the bishop of Rome
Explain why the church of Rome gained special honor among early churches, including its place in the capital and its link to Peter and Paul
Contrast the authority of Scripture as the church's final rule with the authority later claimed by the pope
Describe the medieval church hierarchy of pope, cardinals, bishops, and priests and the role of each
Compare the medieval hierarchy with the offices of elder and deacon described in the New Testament
Analyze the Roman Catholic reading of Matthew 16 as grounds for Petrine supremacy alongside the Reformed reading that the church is built on the confession of Christ
Explain how the collapse of Roman imperial rule in the West left the bishop of Rome as a leading civil and spiritual figure
Describe the contributions of Gregory the Great, including his mission to England, his pastoral writing, and his governing of Rome
Explain how the alliance with Frankish kings, including Pepin's donation and the crowning of Charlemagne in 800, created the Papal States and tied popes to political power
Explain how the Donation of Constantine was used to support papal claims and how Lorenzo Valla showed it to be a forgery
Analyze the Investiture Controversy between Gregory VII and Henry IV and the settlement reached at the Concordat of Worms
Evaluate the claims of Innocent III and Boniface VIII's Unam Sanctam to papal supremacy over earthly rulers in light of Jesus' teaching on his kingdom
Defend the Reformed confessional position that no pope can be head of the church, using Scripture and the Westminster Confession
Construct a historical argument tracing the stages by which the honor of the Roman bishop grew into a claim to universal spiritual and civil jurisdiction

changes: Kept and reworded the real competencies: the pope as Rome's bishop, Rome as capital, Peter and Paul in Rome, the title pope, Leo and Attila, Scripture versus papal authority, the hierarchy, Petrine supremacy, Gregory the Great, the fall of Rome, the Donation of Constantine, the Investiture Controversy, the Protestant rejection, and the synthesis of temporal and spiritual power. Dropped the vague 'church became very powerful' filler and the duplicate evaluation of accumulated papal power, folding it into the grade 12 capstone. Added Christ as head of the church, reasons for Rome's early honor, a comparison with New Testament offices, the Frankish alliance and Papal States, and the claims of Innocent III and Unam Sanctam. Each item now has specific verse references, and Westminster Confession citations appear only where they state the doctrine taught. The Petrine objective now sets out the Roman Catholic and Reformed readings for students to analyze. East-West Schism and late medieval reform material is left to the sibling sub-topics.
